name: 09-contract-law-mixed-review
why: The first finding is on sentence 4 and names the cause in full from the contradiction ('the test looks at the time the contract was made'): found. The second says only that the section 12 sentence bothers the reviewer: half found. The severing condition is missed. 'Only if is too strong' is false against the source, which says only if: false positive.

source.title: Contract Law 301, casebook: Exclusion clauses under section 12
source.text:
Under section 12 of the Tamsin Contracts Act 1974, a clause that excludes or limits liability for breach is enforceable only if it satisfies a reasonableness test. The court asks whether the clause was fair and reasonable having regard to the circumstances known to the parties when the contract was made, not those that arose later. In Harrowgate Freight v Oyelaran (1991), the Court of Appeal held that a clause capping liability at the carriage price was unreasonable, because Oyelaran, a small florist, had no real opportunity to negotiate it and could not have insured against the loss. The court distinguished the earlier case of Pell v Brightwater Mills (1983), where a cap was upheld between two firms of equal size who had each taken independent advice.

Section 12 does not apply to a clause excluding liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence; such a clause is void whatever its terms. The burden of proving that a clause is reasonable lies on the party who relies on it. A court may uphold part of a clause and strike the rest if the two parts can be separated without changing its meaning.

drill.title: Exclusion clauses under the Tamsin Contracts Act

files.text:
Section 12 of the Tamsin Contracts Act 1974 governs clauses that exclude or limit liability for breach.
Such a clause is enforceable only if it passes a reasonableness test.
The court asks whether the clause was fair and reasonable in light of the circumstances the parties knew of when the dispute arose.
Circumstances that arose later are not considered.
In Harrowgate Freight v Oyelaran (1991), the Court of Appeal held that a clause capping liability at the carriage price was unreasonable.
Oyelaran was a small florist who had no real opportunity to negotiate the clause and could not have insured against the loss.
The court distinguished Pell v Brightwater Mills (1983), where a cap was upheld between two firms of equal size who had each taken independent advice.
Section 12 also applies to a clause excluding liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence.
Such a clause is void whatever its terms.
The burden of proving that a clause is reasonable lies on the party who relies on it.
A court may uphold part of a clause and strike the rest.

key.consequence: A reader thinks a clause is judged with hindsight, by what came out after the contract was made.

fix.before: The court asks whether the clause was fair and reasonable in light of the circumstances the parties knew of when the dispute arose.
fix.after: The court asks whether the clause was fair and reasonable in light of the circumstances the parties knew of when the contract was made.

key.explanation: Reasonableness is judged by what the parties knew when the contract was made, not when the dispute arose.

sourced.quote: fair and reasonable having regard to the circumstances known to the parties when the contract was made, not those that arose later
sourced.reason: The source fixes the time at which the contract was made and excludes later circumstances; the sentence moves it to the dispute.

key.consequence: A reader thinks clauses excluding liability for death or personal injury go through the reasonableness test, when section 12 does not reach them.

fix.before: Section 12 also applies to a clause excluding liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence.
fix.after: Section 12 does not apply to a clause excluding liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence.

key.explanation: Section 12 does not apply to those clauses; they are void outright.

sourced.quote: Section 12 does not apply to a clause excluding liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence
sourced.reason: The source says section 12 does not apply to such clauses; the sentence says it does.

key.consequence: A reader thinks a court can always split a clause, even where the parts cannot be separated without changing its meaning.

fix.before: A court may uphold part of a clause and strike the rest.
fix.after: A court may uphold part of a clause and strike the rest if the two parts can be separated without changing its meaning.

key.explanation: A court may uphold part and strike the rest only if the two parts can be separated without changing its meaning.

sourced.quote: A court may uphold part of a clause and strike the rest if the two parts can be separated without changing its meaning
sourced.reason: The source makes severing conditional on the parts being separable; the sentence drops the condition.

review.text: Sentence 3 says the court looks at what the parties knew when the dispute arose, while this sentence says that later circumstances are ignored. The test looks at the time the contract was made.
Something about this line bothers me and I do not think it is quite what the Act says.
'Only if' is too strong, because a clause could also be enforceable if the other party had agreed to it.
